title: Click
full_review:
Michael Newman is as exasperated by the plethora of remote controls at home as most of us, but when he goes to Bed, Bath & Beyond in search of a universal remote control he gets far more than he bargained for.

Such is the concept for "Click" (Columbia/Revolution), a fitfully compelling fantasy about a workaholic architect, Michael (Adam Sandler), whose loving but chaotic home life includes wife Donna (Kate Beckinsale), and kids Ben and Samantha. His warm-hearted parents, Ted (Henry Winkler) and Trudy (Julie Kavner), are completely marginalized with his intense focus on work.

Michael spends increasingly less time with any of them, while his smarmy, inconsiderate boss, Mr. Ammer (David Hasselhoff), piles on the pressure -- projects for demanding Arab and Japanese moguls -- with scant regard for Michael's personal life.

At Bed, Bath & Beyond, he stumbles into the private "Beyond" area (an amusing concept), and discovers a mysterious inventor, Morty (Christopher Walken in Gene Wilder "Willy Wonka" mode), who gives him a remote control, with the caveat that he can never return it. "Why would I return something that's free?" Michael asks. (He'll soon find out.)

At home, Michael discovers he can do all sorts of wondrous things with it, like silencing the dog's barking, and skipping over troublesome family obligations that keep him from his architectural planning. The only problem is, the remote begins to fast-forward his life well beyond his control, hurtling him into the future by leaps and bounds, causing him to miss out on pleasurable moments and family milestones.

Rather like Ebenezer Scrooge or George Bailey in "It's a Wonderful Life," Michael's look into the future is not pretty: His wife has left him, his son has gotten fat, he's beset with health problems and worse. He desperately wants off the merry-go-round, but Morty reminds him there's no returning the remote.

Furthermore, Morty is suddenly revealed to have a sinister side.

Frank Coraci's uneven film -- reminiscent of those other stories -- begins as a comedy (and a fairly crude one at that). Then the movie turns almost tragic when Michael gets a chance to see into the future, leading him to deplore his all-consuming work habits which leads to a life-changing epiphany.

Sandler's performance, too, is a mix of his old-style lowbrow antics and impressive growing maturity. He's quite good in the futuristic scenes with graying hair and a paunch, and shows more depth as an actor than he has before, suggesting it might be time he put away the sophomoric shtick (e.g., passing gas in the boss's face).

The pervasive crude language, even among the children, and some extraneous sexual elements, are regrettable, as is the tasteless humor such as the family dog being, shall we say, a little too "romantic" with a stuffed duck. All in all, writers Steve Koren and Mark O'Keefe should have opted for a classier approach, and made a film appropriate for a much wider audience.

That being said, no one's going to argue with the film's ultimate rousingly affirmative conclusion: Family comes first. There are several remarkably touching moments, but the troublesome elements -- which, unfortunately, viewers can't fast-forward through -- preclude warmer endorsement.

This film contains unneeded vulgar humor including flatulence, innuendo and sexual sight gags, crude language and expressions, profanity, promiscuity, ethnic stereotyping, a transgender character and drug references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
